title: Mongols and Goryeo
description: Mongol conquest, the letter to Changchun, the Tripitaka Koreana, and Goryeo’s resistance and submission. HIST 212 · November 5.
meta: Ebrey 93–96, 162–168, 176–182 · Chinggis Khan · David Morgan · Koryŏ sa

sections.title: Tripitaka Koreana
sections.source: Artwork of the day · Ebrey p.176

body.html:
The Tripitaka Koreana is a collection of Buddhist scriptures carved onto wooden printing blocks. Ink applied to the carved surface produces pages on paper.

81,258 blocks
A Buddhist canon in classical Chinese, preserved at Haeinsa in southern Korea.
Carved during invasion
Goryeo commissioned the replacement collection after the earlier blocks burned in 1232. The work appealed to the Buddha’s protection against the Mongols.
Texts and buildings
The blocks are thirteenth century. The surviving storage buildings are fifteenth century, designed to regulate ventilation and humidity.

UNESCO: the collection · The storage buildings

Dates and location

Ebrey p.176 dates the carving to 1237–1251; UNESCO’s World Heritage description gives 1237–1248. Both place it during the Mongol invasions. Haeinsa is the collection’s present home; its current storage halls were built later. Locate Haeinsa, Ganghwa and Kuju on the map.

body.p: Temujin became Chinggis Khan in 1206. “Genghis Khan” is another English spelling. His achievement was political as well as military: rival groups became a larger army and governing order.

body.html:
1. 1206Temujin recognized as Chinggis Khan.
  2. 1215Mongols capture the Jin capital at present-day Beijing.
  3. 1227Chinggis dies; conquest continues under his successors.
  4. 1279The Southern Song falls, decades after his death.

body.p: Pastoral nomads move herds between grazing grounds. Steppe societies also traded, fought and negotiated with agricultural states. The Mongols inherited this long history; horses alone do not explain their new scale of conquest.

body.html:
Mobility
Mounted forces, spare horses and supplies from herds supported rapid movement over long distances.
Organization
Military units cut across older tribal divisions. Discipline and coordinated command made many groups act together.
Surrender and terror
Submission could preserve local rulers. Resistance risked mass killing. The offer and the threat worked together.
Borrowed expertise
Engineers, siege weapons, administrators and artisans expanded what the conquerors could do.

body.p: Taking a walled city required different skills from winning a cavalry battle. Governing its population required still others. Campaigns against Japan, Vietnam and Java also show the limits of Mongol success.
Wen and wu: wén means civil or cultural accomplishment; wǔ means martial power. The letter to Changchun shows a conqueror seeking authority and expertise beyond warfare.

sections.title: Chinggis Khan invites a Daoist sage
sections.source: Letter dated May 15, 1219 · Bretschneider, vol. I, pp.37–39 · Reader PDF pp.2–4

body.p: Changchun, also known as Qiu Chuji, was a Daoist religious teacher. The letter asks him to travel to the khan. It presents the conqueror as simple, chosen by Heaven and in need of wise assistance.

passage.quote: Heaven has abandoned China owing to its haughtiness and extravagant luxury.
passage.cite: Letter, Bretschneider p.37 · Reader PDF p.2

passage.quote: To cross a river we make boats and rudders. Likewise we invite sage men, and choose out assistants for <mark>keeping the empire in good order</mark>.
passage.cite: Letter, Bretschneider p.38 · Reader PDF p.3

body.p: These are claims made in a Chinese-language letter issued in Chinggis’s name. They show how he sought to persuade a religious authority. They do not by themselves establish how he treated conquered people.

body.html:
Translation, authorship and optional video

E. Bretschneider, Mediæval Researches from Eastern Asiatic Sources, vol. I (1888), pp.37–39. Bretschneider suggests a Chinese adviser composed the wording, but his proposed identification of the writer is uncertain.

Voices of the Past: reading of the letter · 5:37. A modern performance of the source. The excerpts above and the Reader PDF provide the written version.

sections.title: Destruction and the limits of the numbers
sections.source: David Morgan, The Mongols, pp.73–83 · Reader PDF pp.5–15

body.p: Morgan is a modern historian evaluating accounts of conquest. Reports of mass death are evidence, but their numbers need to be tested against population, genre and the writer’s situation.

passage.quote: not as statistical information but as evidence of the state of mind

body.html:
Immediate violence

Killing, enslavement and forced relocation destroyed communities. An implausible total does not make the catastrophe imaginary.

Longer damage

A qanat is an underground channel that brings groundwater to farmland. It requires continual maintenance. The loss or displacement of farming communities could damage agriculture for generations.

body.p: Morgan also stresses variation: some places escaped destruction or later prospered. Neither universal ruin nor universal prosperity describes the whole empire.

body.html:
Tang connections

Chang’an attracted foreign residents, merchants and religious communities. Buddhism, goods and artistic forms crossed Eurasia long before Mongol conquest.

Mongol connections

A larger imperial network supported movement by merchants, envoys and specialists. Some traveled for opportunity; others were taken by force.

Merchants and envoys
Political connections made some long journeys easier.
Artisans and captives
Imperial demand could relocate skilled people against their will.
Disease
Greater movement also helped disease travel.

body.p: Pax Mongolica means “Mongol peace.” The phrase describes conditions that facilitated exchange; it cannot describe every community’s experience of conquest.

sections.title: Goryeo: the court moves to Ganghwa

body.html:
1. 1170Military coup in Goryeo.
  2. 1196Choe Chungheon establishes his family’s dominance.
  3. 1231Mongol invasion; Kuju resists.
  4. 1232The court moves from Gaegyeong to Ganghwa Island.

body.p: The king remained, but the Choe military family controlled the government. Moving the court protected the ruling group while mainland communities bore repeated attacks. Resistance could defend the dynasty and impose severe costs on its people.
The explanation on SKT p.201 is the modern editors’ introduction. The following Kuju narrative is a translated passage from the <cite>Koryŏ sa</cite>, the later history of Goryeo.

sections.title: Kuju: a town holds, the court orders surrender
sections.source: Koryŏ sa 103:23a–26a · SKT 202–203 · Reader PDF p.17

body.p: Pak Sŏ commanded the defense of Kuju in 1231. The account describes defenders answering successive siege methods with repairs and countermeasures.

passage.quote: chained iron links across the holes and repaired them
passage.cite: Koryŏ sa excerpt, SKT p.203 · Reader PDF p.17

body.html:
At the walls

Pak Sŏ keeps resisting. Local military success gives him a reason to continue.

At court

The king orders surrender. The commander’s duty to defend the town now conflicts with obedience to his ruler.

passage.cite: Koryŏ sa excerpt, SKT p.203 · Reader PDF p.17

body.p: Pak Sŏ finally yields to the order. The town’s defense and the state’s diplomatic settlement operate at different scales. This is a later historical account of the siege, not a transcript recorded at the walls.

sections.title: What Goryeo kept, and what it paid

body.html:
The dynasty survives

Peace in 1259 and the court’s return to the mainland in 1270 lead to a subordinate relationship. Goryeo keeps its royal dynasty, unlike the defeated Southern Song.

Independence is limited

Royal marriages tie Goryeo to the Mongol ruling house. Its rulers supply resources and ships for campaigns against Japan, while Mongol influence shapes aristocratic life.

body.p: Conquest did not produce one political arrangement everywhere. Goryeo’s surviving dynasty was compatible with dependence on the Mongol empire.
